The Ballroom  with its one-tonne chandelier (12,000 crystals) given to Canada by England for its aid in the Second World War. This is where cabinet ministers are sworn in and medals of bravery are awarded.
The portrait on the back wall is the Diamond Jubilee Portrait of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II.

images.caption: The Pauline Vanier Room is a small sitting room where informal meetings are held with visiting heads of state and other officials. The room was originally created in the 1960s by Pauline Vanier out of an old aide-de-camp smoking room, putting up pine panelling and filling it with antique furnishings from Quebec. However, it was later again refurbished to remove the tongue and groove planks Vanier had installed and which were said to be reminiscent of suburban basement panelling popular in the 1970s. The Pauline Vanier Room today contains furniture and other cabinetry works by Canadian artisans.

images.caption: Stained glass window to the right of the entrance, marking the first appointment of a Canadian-born governor general; the viceregal position is symbolized by a crowned lion holding a maple leaf and surrounded by the shields of the arms of the first seven persons to hold the post.

images.caption: The Royal Window—a stained glass piece commemorating the 40th anniversary of the accession of Elizabeth II to the throne, displaying, between the Queen's Canadian royal standard above and the Great Seal of Canada below, the monarch's coat of arms for Canada surrounded by the shields of each of the provincial coats of arms. Additionally, in the top two corners are images of Elizabeth's royal cypher, balancing out representations of the Sovereign's badges for both the Order of Canada and the Order of Military Merit in the bottom two corners.

images.caption:
Since I was in the area I decided to visit the Governor General but to my disappointment she wasn't home........ Went inside but it is a very limited tour.
Rideau Hall is, since 1867, the official residence in Ottawa of the Canadian monarch (currently King Charles III) as well as the monarch’s representative, the Governor General of Canada. It is in a 0.36 km2 (88 acre) estate, with the main building consisting of approximately 175 rooms across 9,500 m2 (102,000 sq ft), and 27 outbuildings around the grounds.
Most of Rideau Hall is used for state affairs, only 500 m2 (5,400 sq ft) of its area being dedicated to private living quarters, while additional areas serve as the offices and the principal workplace of the governor general and staff.

Rideau Hall and the surrounding grounds were designated as a National Historic Site of Canada in 1977. The house is open to the public for guided tours throughout the year; approximately 200,000 visitors tour Rideau Hall annually.
